title: Insights and challenges in using C. elegans for investigation of fat metabolism.
text_summary: 本研究旨在探讨秀丽线虫在脂肪代谢研究中的应用。通过综述秀丽线虫脂肪领域的最新进展，重点关注线虫脂滴、脂肪酶、自噬和寿命之间的复杂联系，以及协调脂质稳态的关键转录调控机制分析，揭示了哺乳动物和秀丽线虫脂肪调控途径的古老起源，并突出了秀丽线虫在识别和分析新型脂质途径中的应用。尽管秀丽线虫具有许多优势，但其脂肪调控研究目前仍面临许多概念和方法上的挑战。本研究对领域中的某些假设进行了批判性评估，并强调了在解释秀丽线虫脂质含量数据时应考虑的问题。研究发现，秀丽线虫脂滴在形态和分子特征上与其他物种的脂滴相似，并揭示了秀丽线虫实验的优势，有效地识别了脂滴大小和功能的保守调节因子。此外，研究还发现，自噬和脂肪酸脱饱和对于秀丽线虫的长寿至关重要，并揭示了脂解与自噬途径之间的相互作用。此外，研究还强调了转录因子在协调代谢途径中的作用，如SBP-1、NHR-49和KLF等。然而，在解释秀丽线虫脂质测量结果时，仍存在一些未解决的问题，例如将秀丽线虫肠道与哺乳动物脂肪细胞等同起来，以及将肠道中不同的中性脂质库视为等效的脂质储存。总之，秀丽线虫作为一种研究脂肪代谢的有力模型，为理解脂质稳态、衰老机制以及与代谢相关的其他生物学过程提供了重要见解。

REVIEW ARTICLE
Insights and challenges in using C. elegans for investigation of fat
metabolism
George A. Lemieux and Kaveh Ashrafi
Department of Physiology, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA
Abstract
C. elegans provides a genetically tractable system for deciphering the homeostatic mechanisms
that underlie fat regulation in intact organisms. Here, we provide an overview of the recent
advances in the C. elegans fat field with particular attention to studies of C. elegans lipid
droplets, the complex links between lipases, autophagy, and lifespan, and analyses of key
transcriptional regulatory mechanisms that coordinate lipid homeostasis. These studies
demonstrate the ancient origins of mammalian and C. elegans fat regulatory pathways and
highlight how C. elegans is being used to identify and analyze novel lipid pathways that are
then shown to function similarly in mammals. Despite its many advantages, study of fat
regulation in C. elegans is currently faced with a number of conceptual and methodological
challenges. We critically evaluate some of the assumptions in the field and highlight issues that
we believe should be taken into consideration when interpreting lipid content data in
C. elegans.
Keywords
C. elegans, fat, lipase, lipid, metabolism,
Nile Red, transcription factor

Introduction
Fat regulation is a physiological process
Obesity is a significant risk factor for major diseases
including type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, hyperten-
sion and certain forms of cancer (Bray, 2008; Bray & Wilson,
2008; Kopelman, 2000). The prevailing paradigm for under-
standing obesity views its development as a consequence of
over consumption of nutrients and a sedentary lifestyle. While
food intake and energy expenditure can affect fat content of an
organism, the problem with this nearly universally accepted
conceptualization is that it largely ignores the wealth of well-
established data showing that fat regulation in intact organ-
isms is a physiological process (Atkinson, 2014; Taubes,
2012).
As a physiological process, fat regulation involves an
intertwined set of behavioral, hormonal, and metabolic
responses that act in a homeostatic fashion to maintain
energy balance despite fluctuations in nutrient availability or
demand. This is consistent with the observation that weight
loss is challenging for the vast majority of people and that
most people regain lost weight despite intensive behavioral
treatment (Stunkard & McLaren-Hume, 1959; Wadden et al.,
2011). The recognition that fat regulation is a physiological
process does not ignore the role of environment or behavior in
obesity. However, to fully appreciate the causes of obesity or
develop effective remedies for it, it is then imperative to
understand how environmental triggers interact with physio-
logical mechanisms of fat regulation.
In order to survive and thrive under conditions where
nutrients are in flux, an organism must have ways of sensing
its energetic demands and supplies and be able to adjust its
various functions accordingly. Over the past twenty years
numerous short- and long-term signals of energy balance have
been discovered and studied intensively, generally in murine
models (Nilsson et al., 2012; Schneeberger et al., 2014;
Woods, 2009). Nevertheless, there is still much that is
unknown in terms of how behavior, physiology, and metab-
olism are integrated. Similarly, cell biological mechanisms
that are involved in uptake, transport, and storage of nutrients
as well as the regulatory mechanisms that coordinate complex
catabolic and anabolic responses remain an open area
of investigation. Importantly, the intersection of metabolic
pathways with those involved in normal growth, development,
and aging as well as numerous pathophysiological conditions
remains one of the most pressing areas of research.
It is within this context of energy balance as a physio-
logical process that C. elegans has emerged as a powerful
model system. The same parameters that made C. elegans
useful in deciphering fundamental aspects of cell biology,
developmental biology, and neurobiology – chiefly its
amenability to rapid experimentation, especially genetic
analyses – underlie the utility of this organism for under-
standing the physiology of fat regulation.
Below, we will first discuss the general similarities and
differences between mammalian and C. elegans fat regulatory
pathways and then summarize recent findings from C. elegans
studies. Even in a relatively small field such as that of

C. elegans metabolism, it is impractical to provide a
comprehensive cataloging of all of the efforts in the field in
this one review or an extensive background section to the
wide range of molecular pathways that are being investigated
in C. elegans. The focus in this review will be on cell
biological aspects of lipid deposition and utilization as well as
coordinated regulation of metabolic pathways through tran-
scription factors. These studies provide an excellent demon-
stration of the conservation of C. elegans and mammalian
lipid biology pathways and how C. elegans studies are
revealing links between lipid biology and aging. Although
C. elegans is also being used to delineate neural mechanisms
of feeding behavior and fat regulation and as a system for
identification of small molecules that affect fat and feeding
through phenotypic screening, these topics will not be
covered here.
Despite the many attributes of C. elegans as an organism
for discovering and understanding of fat regulatory pathways,
it is also faced with several conceptual and experimental
challenges. There have been a number of publications that
advocate for use of certain methodologies and call into
questions the validity of other methodologies (Brooks et al.,
2009; O’Rourke et al., 2009; Yen et al., 2010; Zhang et al.,
2010a). Therefore, we believe that the field and those
interested in joining it would benefit from knowing the
precise methodologies and their associated weaknesses and
advantages that are used to assess fat content in C. elegans.
An extensive discussion of these issues is provided.
Overview of C. elegans as a model for studying
fat biology
Since energy balance is fundamental to organism survival,
many of its underlying organizational principles and molecu-
lar mechanisms are deeply conserved across phylogeny. For
instance, in C. elegans as in mammals, changes in food
availability elicit
myriad
behavioral,
physiological,
and
metabolic responses such as those involved in food intake
rate and foraging behaviors (Avery & Horvitz, 1990; De Bono
& Maricq, 2005; Greer et al., 2008; Hills et al., 2004; Sawin
et al., 2000; You et al., 2008, 2006), likelihood of mating
(Lipton et al., 2004), and alterations in expression and
activity of fat metabolic pathways and composition of fat
stores (Brock et al., 2006; McKay et al., 2003; Taubert
et al., 2006; Van Gilst et al., 2005a). These food-evoked
behaviors are not merely reflexes to nutritional signals since
they can be entrained by experience (Sawin et al., 2000;
Shtonda & Avery, 2006; You et al., 2008). Moreover, food
deprivation promotes utilization of C. elegans fat stores and
fat content of C. elegans is subject to change based on their
nutrient supply (Brooks et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2014).
At the molecular level, evolutionarily conserved fat and
feeding mechanisms in C. elegans and humans range from
mechanisms that underlie lipid uptake, packaging, transport
and storage in the form of lipid droplets as well as those
involved in liberation of stored lipids and their breakdown for
generation of energy through fat oxidation pathways (Ashrafi,
2007; Ashrafi et al., 2003; Brock et al., 2007; McKay et al.,
2003; Shtonda & Avery, 2006; Taubert et al., 2006; Van Gilst
et al., 2005a,b). As in mammals, these core metabolic
functions are regulated by a sophisticated and intricate set
of transcription factors including nuclear hormone receptors
and the SREBP transcription factor (Brock et al., 2007, 2006;
McKay et al., 2003; Taubert et al., 2006; Van Gilst et al.,
2005a,b; Yang et al., 2006). In turn, cellular fuel gauge
mechanisms such as TOR and AMPK kinase complexes
orchestrate cellular responses (Apfeld et al., 2004; Beale,
2008; Jia et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2008;
Meissner et al., 2004; Schulz et al., 2007; Soukas et al.,
2009; Vellai et al., 2003). Moreover, the worm’s metabolic
and physiological responses are coordinated through various
endocrine regulators such as such as insulin signaling
(Fielenbach
&
Antebi,
2008;
Kimura
et al.,
1997;
Mukhopadhyay
et al.,
2005,
2006;
Taguchi
&
White,
2008). Finally, neural mechanisms such as serotonin, dopa-
mine, oxytocin, and glutamate pathways regulate feeding rate
or foraging strategies of C. elegans (Beets et al., 2012; Greer
et al., 2008; Hills et al., 2004; Lemieux et al., 2013; Sawin
et al., 2000; Sze et al., 2000) but can also affect fat
metabolism independently of effects on feeding behavior
through initiation of neuroendocrine cascades (Cunningham
et al., 2014, 2012; Noble et al., 2013; Srinivasan et al.,
2008). There is also evidence that, in C. elegans as in
mammals, the energetic state of the periphery is commu-
nicated to the nervous system (Bendena et al., 2008; Janssen
et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2008; You et al., 2008).
Further suggesting the ancient evolutionary origins of
fat and feeding pathways is the finding that a number of
genes, which when mutated cause obesity in humans, have
C. elegans counterparts with roles in feeding behavior and
metabolism. Examples include the BBS genes, which underlie
the obesity associated Bardet-Biedl syndrome in humans (Lee
et al., 2011; Mak et al., 2006), and the transcription factor
SIM-1, which in humans is involved in the development of
specific regions of the hypothalamus and mutations in it
are associated with obesity (Michaud et al., 2001). Finally,
C. elegans fat and feeding can be modulated by compounds,
such as fluoxetine and AMPK-activators, that are known to
alter mammalian fat content and feeding behavior (Lemieux
et al., 2011; Srinivasan et al., 2008). In the sections below,
we will highlight studies in C. elegans that have led to the
discovery of previously unappreciated components of mam-
malian fat biology.
There are also, of course, numerous differences between
mammalian and C. elegans fat biology. Certain molecular
pathways that are relevant to mammalian fat biology, for
example leptin signaling, are either entirely lacking or very
rudimentary in C. elegans. It does not have dedicated
adipocytes. However, C. elegans homologs of some of the
genes that underlie mammalian adipocyte differentiation and
function also modulate intestinal and skin-like fat depots, the
main sites of fat storage in C. elegans (Ashrafi et al., 2003;
Brock et al., 2006; Hellerer et al., 2007; Kimura et al.,
1997; McKay et al., 2003; Van Gilst et al., 2005b).
Lipid droplets of C. Elegans
Lipid droplets are subcellular organelles that store neutral
lipids (Walther & Farese, 2012). They have a core that is
enriched in hydrophobic lipids such as triacylglycerides and
cholesterol esters of fatty acids and surrounded by a
monolayer of phospholipids. A number of enzymes involved

in neutral lipid synthesis are associated with the ER
membrane. Accordingly, lipid droplets are thought to form
in discrete regions between the two leaflets of the ER
membrane. In general, it is thought that these nascent droplets
grow and eventually bud out of the ER (Walther & Farese,
2012). However, it has been suggested that lipid droplets,
once formed, remain wholly enveloped by an outstretched
ER membrane (Jacquier et al., 2011).
In C. elegans, substantial fat deposits exist in both the
intestine and hypodermis and maturing oocytes of the
germline as well as fertilized embryos that have not yet
been laid as eggs (Figure 1). In certain mutants or aged
animals, lipid droplets are also seen in muscle (Herndon
et al., 2002). By electron microscopy lipid droplets of
C. elegans, as those of mammals, appear as electron translu-
cent structures contained within a phospholipid monolayer
(Zhang et al., 2010b). Several enzymes with evolutionarily
conserved function in regulating lipid droplet biology are
associated with the C. elegans lipid droplets, including
homologs of adipose tissue triglyceride lipase (ATGL-1),
seipin, and diacyl glyceride acyl transferases (DGAT-1
and -2) and stearoyl CoA desaturases (FAT-6 and -7)
(Klemm et al., 2013; Mullaney et al., 2010; Shi et al.,
2013; Xu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2010a).
Purification and proteomic analysis of lipid droplets from
C. elegans identified 306 proteins associated with this
compartment (Zhang et al., 2012). A majority of these
proteins (63%) were orthologous to known mammalian
proteins that had been shown to be lipid droplet-associated
in previous studies. The authors confirmed that a protein
orthologous to short-chain dehydrogenases (DHS-3) was
almost exclusively colocalized with C. elegans lipid droplets.
Despite this impressive degree of conservation of lipid droplet
proteins, not all such proteins are found in the C. elegans
genome. For instance, there are no obvious orthologs of
perilipins or CIDE-family proteins, although functionally
orthologous proteins may yet be found. Indeed, expression
of a GFP-fusion of Drosophila perilipin-1 (PLIN1) in the
C. elegans intestine was recently shown to localize to lipid
droplets and serve as a readout for an RNAi-based screen for
genes that alter lipid droplet size and abundance (Liu et al.,
2014).
Molecular components involved in the control of lipid
droplet size have been identified through forward genetic
screens in C. elegans. Mutants defective in peroxisomal beta-
oxidation (maoc-1, dhs-28, daf-22 and prx-10) have enlarged
lipid droplets whose size in contrast to wild-type animals is not
influenced by fasting or over expression of ATGL-1 (Zhang
et al., 2010a). In the same study it was found that dietary
influences also controls lipid droplet size. Feeding C. elegans
the HB101 strain of E. coli rather than the standard lab strain of
OP50 E. coli resulted in animals with reduced lipid droplet
size. This effect was dependent on the production of vaccenic
acid, which HB101 bacteria lack (Zhang et al., 2010a).
Another screen was based on the observation that loss-of-
function mutations in daf-22 cause expansion of C. elegans
lipid droplets and excess accumulation of triglycerides
(Xu et al., 2012). daf-22 encodes a sterol carrier protein
orthologous to human SCP-2, an enzymatic component of
peroxisomal beta-oxidation. In a mutagenesis screen, alleles
of acs-22, encoding a fatty acyl-CoA synthetase, and dgat-2,
encoding a diacylglyceride acyl transferase, were found to
suppress the expanded lipid droplet phenotype of daf-22
mutants. The C. elegans orthologs of ACS-22 and DGAT-2
were shown to physically interact and form a complex at the
interface of the ER and associated lipid droplets. Specifically,
GFP-tagged ACS-22 was ER-localized and DGAT-2 was
localized to lipid droplets. The lipid droplet localization of
DGAT-2 was critical since expression of an ER-tethered
DGAT-2 failed to induce large lipid droplets in daf-22; dgat-2
double mutants. Conservation of mechanisms of lipid droplet
formation between C. elegans and mammals was highlighted
by the finding that mammalian FATP1, an acs-22 homolog,
also colocalizes with the mammalian DGAT-2 on lipid
droplets in COS-7 cells and promotes enlargement of lipid
droplet size (Xu et al., 2012).
Finally, another screen took advantage of the observation
that a GFP fusion to the C. elegans ortholog of seipin, which
in mammals is associated with lipid droplets, labels a subset
of intestinal lipid droplets (Klemm et al., 2013). This led to
the discovery that inactivation of atln-1 decreased lipid
droplet size but increased the number of lipid droplets in
C. elegans intestinal cells and resulted in an overall 30%
decrease in extractable triglycerides. atln-1 is a C. elegans
ortholog of the vertebrate atlastin family of proteins which are
ER-localized members of the dynamin family of GTPases
with roles in ER morphology and maintenance. The involve-
ment of atlastin in lipid droplet enlargement was confirmed in
both the Drosophila fat body and in mammalian cells. Since
atlastin is ER localized but not associated with lipid droplets,
its effects on lipid droplet size were attributed to its activity in
regulating ER membrane fusion.
These studies clearly show that lipid droplets of C. elegans
share both morphological as well as molecular characteristics
with this organelle from other species. More importantly,
these studies are an excellent demonstration of how the amen-
ability of C. elegans to experimentation can be effectively
harnessed to identify conserved regulators of lipid droplets’
size and function.
Lipid utilization, lipases, autophagy and lifespan
Lipases are a diverse class of enzymes that catalyze the
hydrolysis of triacylglycerols (Zechner et al., 2012). They
include secreted, digestive lipases, cell-surface anchored
lipases, and intracellular neutral and acid lipases (Kersten,
2014;
Wang et al.,
2013;
Zechner et al., 2012).
The
C. elegans genome encodes numerous lipases, however, the
C. elegans counterparts of intracellular neutral and acid
lipases have received the most attention. Particular focus has
been on understanding the molecular links between lipases,
induction of autophagy, and extension of organism’s lifespan.
Autophagy and lipid metabolism
Extended periods of food deprivation in mammals induce
autophagy as a energy generating strategy, however, it is now
becoming clear that a lysosomal degradative pathway of
autophagy, named lipophagy, is also involved in normal lipid
homeostasis such that inhibition of the process leads to excess
accumulation of lipids (Liu & Czaja, 2013). Similar to these

observations in mammalian systems, inactivation of autop-
hagy genes in C. elegans results in enhanced staining of gut
granules or lysosome related organelles during fasting (Huang
et al., 2014). In contrast to this though, it has been reported
that inactivation of autophagy genes in C. elegans results in
reduction of lipid stores when assessed by other methods
(Lapierre et al., 2013b). The precise mechanistic reasons for
these opposite outcomes are not yet clear. However, as
summarized below, a number of likely acid lipases regulate
lipid levels in C. elegans in a manner analogous to the role
of lipophagy in mammals.
LIPL-1, LIPL-2, LIPL-3 and LIPL-5
Expression of a group of predicted triacylglyceride lipases
encoded by lipl-1, -2, -3, -4, and -5, is upregulated 2–45-fold
by fasting (O’Rourke & Ruvkun, 2013). Using an RNAi-
based screen for transcription factors that alter the expression
of lipl-1 the authors found that inactivation of the mxl-3,
encoding a MAX-like-3 basic-helix-loop-helix transcription
factor, led to transcriptional upregulation of all of these
lipases except that of lipl-4 in well fed animals. Intestinal cells
and sensory neurons express mxl-3 and inactivation of mxl-3
specifically in the intestine was sufficient for the noted
transcriptional effects. Interestingly, MXL-3 is localized in
the nuclei of intestinal cells in ad libitum fed animals, is lost
after short term fasting (2–6 h) but is re-expressed, accom-
panied by a drop in expressions of the noted lipases, in
12–18 h fasted animals. These findings suggested that MXL-3
represses expression of the lipl genes and loss of mxl-3 is part
of an acute phase response to fasting.
Since MXL-3 binds to the same promoter sequence and
regulates similar genes as another basic-helix-loop-helix
transcription factor, HLH-30, investigation of hlh-30 during
fasting revealed that its expression is induced during similar
fasting intervals over which mxl-3 was repressed. Consistent
with this, hlh-30 was required for the full up-regulation of
lipl genes. This was the case even in mxl-3 mutants.
C. elegans bearing hlh-30 mutations do not lose fat during
starvation as rapidly as their wildtype counterparts and have
severe defects in starvation survival both as larvae and as
adults (O’Rourke & Ruvkun, 2013; Settembre et al., 2013).
Thus, the MXL-3/HLH-30 toggle represents a transcriptional
fasting response switch.
The mammalian ortholog of hlh-30 is transcription factor
EB, TFEB, which regulates autophagy, a processes involved
in both lipid utilization and aging (Lapierre et al., 2013a;

&
Ruvkun,
2013;
Settembre
et al.,
2013).
Consistent with this, hlh-30 regulates expression of genes
involved in autophagy and is required for extended lifespans
of multiple C. elegans mutants. Unlike its transcriptional
regulation of lipl genes, HLH-30 mediated regulation of
autophagy genes is not antagonized by MXL-3. Nevertheless,
mxl-3 mutants are long-lived, a phenotype dependent on hlh-
30 as well as simultaneous presence of both lipl-1 and lipl-3
genes (O’Rourke & Ruvkun, 2013).
LIPL-4
Reduction of function mutations in daf-2 and glp-1 cause
some of the most profound effects on lifespan extension in
C. elegans (Lapierre & Hansen, 2012). daf-2 encodes for an
insulin receptor like protein while glp-1 encodes a LIN12/
notch receptor family protein critical for germ cell prolifer-
ation (Byrd & Kimble, 2009; Murphy & Hu, 2013). As adults,
both daf-2 and glp-1 have elevated levels of extractable
triglycerides but reduced levels of Nile Red vital dye staining,
an observation that has been used to call into question the
utility of Nile Red for analysis of C. elegans lipid metabolism
(O’Rourke et al., 2009; Yen et al., 2010); (see section below
for extended discussion on this discrepancy). Suppression of
the low Nile Red staining of glp-1 was used to search for
genes that could shed light on mechanisms that underlie
the extended lifespan of these mutants (Wang et al., 2008).
This led to identification of lipl-4, a triglyceride lipase of the
lysosomal acid lipase family. Transcription of lipl-4 was
found to be upregulated in both glp-1 and daf-2 mutants and
the extended lifespans of both of these mutants required lipl-4
(Wang et al., 2008). Moreover, ectopic overexpression of
lipl-4 in the intestine was sufficient to extend the lifespan of
otherwise wildtype animals. Finally, transcriptional upregula-
tion of lipl-4 in both glp-1 and daf-2 mutants depended on
daf-16, encoding a FOXO family transcription factor, which is
inhibited by insulin signaling (Ogg et al., 1997). The authors
of this study concluded that loss of the germline promotes
systemic lipolysis that in turn promotes longevity.
Another study found that mRNA of mechanistic Target-
Of-Rapamycin-1, mTORC-1, is repressed in glp-1 mutants,
leading to induction of autophagy gene expression through the
FOXA transcription factor PHA-4. In turn, pha-4 was shown
to be essential for the extended longevity phenotype of glp-1
animals (Lapierre et al., 2011). Interestingly, the induction of
lipl-4 lipase is required for activation of autophagy in glp-1
animals and overexpression of lipl-4 is sufficient to initiate
autophagy induction (Lapierre et al., 2011). A clue as to the
role of lipl-4 is suggested by the finding that a metabolic
consequence of lipl-4 overexpression or induction during
fasting is the production of !-6 fatty acids, which induce
autophagy, promote starvation survival and extend lifespan of
animals (O’Rourke et al., 2013).
Since autophagy is required for the extended longevity of
both
glp-1
and
daf-2
mutants
(Lapierre
et al.,
2011;
Mele´ndez et al., 2003) these results clearly indicate a role
for lipolysis in regulating lifespan through crosstalk with
autophagy pathways. However, an unresolved issue in the
literature is why glp-1 or daf-2 animals, which have elevated
levels of autophagy, also exhibit highly elevated levels of
extractable triglycerides. A framework for thinking about this
apparent discrepancy is provided in another section (below).
LIPL-17
Another predicted lipase, lipl-17, is also upregulated in its
expression and needed for the extended lifespan of glp-1
mutants (McCormick et al., 2012). As in the case of lipl-4,
upregulation of lipl-17 requires daf-16. However, unlike lipl-
4, upregulation of lipl-17 also requires the steroid hormone
receptor,
DAF-12.
Finally,
glp-1
mutants
also
exhibit
upregulation of another transcription factor encoded by nhr-
80, which in turn, is required for transcriptional upregulation
of fat-6, encoding a fatty acid desaturase (Brock et al., 2006;

required for the extended lifespan of glp-1 animals leading to

Together, these studies indicate that both autophagy and
fatty acid desaturation are needed for the long lifespan of
glp-1 mutants. Additionally, there are multiple transcription
factors and other signaling pathways such as TOR signaling
that link nutritional status or a loss of germ-line stem cells to
upregulation of autophagy and activation of various lipid
homeostatic mechanisms. These transcription factors appear
to have both overlapping and distinct roles, perhaps reflecting
the fact that autophagy, lipid utilization, and lipid desaturation
may be common outcomes in response to numerous changes
in nutritional status and genetic mutations that perturb
metabolism. Importantly, some of the lipase studies in these
contexts appear to be required for initiation of autophagic
responses. One possibility is that different lipases help
generate lipid messengers that then coordinate various
transcriptional and cellular responses.
LIPS-7
Inactivation of the C. elegans ortholog of the NAD(H)-
regulated C-teminal binding protein-1 (ctbp-1) results in a
reduction in fat content, an extension of lifespan and the
uregulation of more then 200 transcripts including a predicted
triacylglyceride lipase, lips-7 (Chen et al., 2009). Inactivation
of lips-7 abrogated both the reduced fat content and the
lifespan extension phenotype of ctbp-1 mutants. These
observations provided one of the first insights into the
regulation of lifespan in response to the induction of lipase
activity.
ATGL
Adipose triglyceride lipase, ATGL, catalyzes the conversion
of triacylglycerides to diacylglycerides, the first step in
liberation of stored neutral lipids (Zechner et al., 2012). The
C. elegans genome encodes a homolog of this lipase, which
localizes to lipid droplets and its over expression leads to
their size reduction (Mullaney et al., 2010; Zhang et al.,
2010a).
In response to poor environmental conditions such as low
food availability and high population density, second larval
stage C. elegans exit reproductive growth and enter dauer
arrest (Hu, 2007). As animals prepare for the dauer stage, they
accumulate large fat reservoirs, which presumably function as
a source of energy during this non-feeding state (Hu, 2007).
Dauers deficient in aak-2, encoding for one of the two
catalytic subunits of AMP-activated kinase, AMPK, were
found to rapidly lose their fat stores (Narbonne & Roy, 2009).
Moreover, it was found that C. elegans atgl is required for this
fat loss and that AAK-2 can phosphorylate ATGL-derived
peptides, which led to the suggestion that AAK-2 functions to
ration lipid utilization through its regulation of ATGL
specifically during the dauer state (Narbonne & Roy, 2009).
However, the specific role of aak-2 in regulation of dauer fat
has more recently been called into question as it was shown
that aak-2 mutants have reduced fat levels at all stages and
that reconstitution of aak-2 in the nervous system only was
sufficient to confer normal fat storage to aak-2 mutants
(Cunningham et al., 2014). Elevated serotonin signaling
leads to inactivation of neural AAK-2 (Cunningham et al.,
2012) and promotes a neuroendocrine cascade leading to
peripheral fat reduction due to enhanced fat oxidation

Consistent with this, atgl transcription was shown to be
upregulated upon elevation of serotonin (Noble et al., 2013)
providing an alternative explanation for the observed regula-

C05D11.7, which is designated as the C. elegans counter-
part of ATGL, is also a close homolog of another neutral
lipase, PNPLA5. The PNPLA5 lipase is thought to act
on lipid droplets to provide substrates for the synthesis of
phospholipids that are required autophagosome membrane
formation (Dupont et al., 2014).
UPR, lipases, and starvation survival
The ER is increasingly being recognized as a key organelle
in regulating lipogenesis via the components classically-
associated with the unfolded protein response, UPR (Zhou &
Liu, 2014). Key molecular components of mammalian UPR
include IRE1 and its regulator BiP. The C. elegans counter-
parts of these components, ire-1 and hsp-4, were shown to be
required for fasting-induced fat loss, which was demonstrated
through vital Nile Red and biochemical extraction methods
(Jo et al., 2009). Moreover, this fasting-induced fat loss
was found to be dependent on two lipases, encoded by fil-1
and fil-2, whose induction depended on ire-1 and hsp-4
(Jo et al., 2009).
In another study, it was shown that losses of polyunsat-
urated fatty acids, PUFAs, and phosphatidyl choline as well as
increases in saturated fats triggers the unfolded protein
response in the endoplasmic reticulum (UPRER) as assessed
by induction of an hsp-4 transcriptional reporter (Hou et al.,
2014). Loss of mdt-15, encoding an ortholog of the ARC105/
mediator complex was shown to change the composition of
triglycerides and phospholipids without affecting their total
levels. Interestingly, the hsp-4 transcriptional response was
independent of any measurable effect on proteostasis and was
independent of a mitochondria unfolded protein response. The
results suggest that membrane fluidity or composition is
directly sensed by UPRER. Activation of UPRER by inde-
pendent inputs may reflect that the ER is a central hub for
both lipid and protein production.

NHR-49 and associated partners
The families of nuclear hormone receptors (NHRs) are
transcription factors that coordinate numerous aspects of
metazoan metabolism. Compared to the human genome,
which encodes 48 NHRs, the C. elegans genome encodes 284.
Most of these (269) represent an expansion of an ancestral
HNF4 family member receptor. The remaining 15 receptors
have clear counterparts in other species (Taubert et al.,
2011).
The C. elegans nuclear hormone receptor encoded by
nhr-49 is a key regulator of fasting induced lipid catabolism.
Increased transcription of genes that encode beta-oxidation
enzymes and the phospholipase IPLA-2 during fasting
requires nhr-49 (Huang et al., 2014; Van Gilst et al.,
2005b). Mutants in nhr-49 have elevated intestinal Nile Red
staining, a vital dye that has been used as an indirect measure

reduced rates of oxygen consumption (Pathare et al., 2012),
two parameters that are consistent with a reduced catabolic
capacity (Van Gilst et al., 2005b). Thus, while by sequence
nhr-49 is most closely related to the HNF-4a family of
transcription factors, in the context of regulation of metab-

Kru¨ppel-like factors
Kru¨ppel-like factors are a class of transcription factors
containing multiple C2H2 zinc-fingers that have roles in
adipocyte differentiation. The C. elegans genome encodes
three genes that are orthologous to their mammalian counter-
parts klf-1, -2, -3. Of the three klf genes, klf-3 mutants have
been reported to have elevated intestinal fat levels, altered fatty
acid desaturation, and altered expression of genes that control
fatty acid desaturation and beta-oxidation (Zhang et al., 2009).
They also exhibit a low-penetrance sterility, with the remaining
fertile animals exhibiting dramatically decreased brood sizes.
Mutants in klf-3 have depressed levels of C. elegans orthologs
of microsomal triglyceride transferase and apolipoprotein B,
dsc-4 and vit-5 which suggests that the elevated levels of
intestinal triglycerides in klf-3 mutants may stem from a defect
in the ability to package this fat into lipoprotein complexes to
send to the developing germline (Zhang et al., 2013).
Regulation of C. elegans metabolism by acyl-CoA
synthetases
Fatty acyl CoA synthetases activate fatty acids by catalyzing
the attachment of co-enzyme A to them (Grevengoed et al.,
2014). This step is required for utilization of fatty acids in
both anabolic and catabolic pathways. Additionally, fatty
acyl-CoAs may serve as signaling molecules (Wellen &
Thompson, 2012). The C. elegans genome encodes over
twenty fatty acyl CoA synthetases but functions for only a few
have been ascribed. This includes a role for acs-1 in
reproduction (Kniazeva et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2011),
acs-20, and acs-22 in cuticle formation (Kage-Nakadai et al.,
2010), acs-2 in fasting induced fat catabolism (Van Gilst
et al., 2005a), and acs-4, and acs-5 in serotonin promoted
beta-oxidation (Srinivasan et al., 2008). Please note that the
nomenclature of the C. elegans ACS family does not
necessarily follow that of mammals so that the worm acs-4
may or may not the closest counterpart of mammalian acs-4.
Animals deficient in acs-3 have enlarged lipid droplets as
visualized by multiple different methods and elevated levels
of dietary fat uptake and de novo fat synthesis (Mullaney
et al., 2010). ACS-3 has long chain fatty acyl CoA synthetase
activity. Curiously, acs-3 is prominently expressed in seam
cells and restoration of wildtype acs-3 in only the seam cells
of acs-3 mutants was sufficient to restore the metabolic
phenotype of this mutant (Mullaney et al., 2010). Seam cells
are a specialized cell type that is part of the skin of the
animal, has some stem-cell characteristics, and is not a depot
where triglycerides are obviously stored or utilized. Extensive
genetic suppressor screening revealed that the metabolic
phenotypes of acs-3 mutants required nhr-25, which is also
expressed in the seam cells (Mullaney et al., 2010). NHR-25
is a member of the NR5A family of receptors its closest
homologs being Drosophila FTZ-F1 and mammalian ster-
oidogenic factor-1, SF-1 and liver receptor homolog-1,
LRH-1. Like its mammalian homologs NHR-25 is able to
bind phospho-inositides containing long chain fatty acids
which suggested a model by which ACS-3 is involved
in generating ligands that modulate NHR-25’s activity. In
analogy to SF-1, NHR-25 activity may lead to generation of
additional hormonal mediators, which in turn, would influ-
ence lipid uptake, synthesis, and storage, all of which occur in
tissues other than the seam cells. In this analogy seam cells
may share functions that are similar to the mammalian
adrenal cortex.
Methods for measuring C. elegans lipids
Diverse methods of assessing experimental alterations to lipid
metabolism in C. elegans have been employed. There are
currently a number of disagreements as to which methods are
most suitable for the analysis of fat content in worms. Since
each method is not without its caveats to implementation and
interpretation, it is certainly worthwhile to employ several of
these methods to analyze the lipid metabolic phenotype of the
organism. However, it is also inappropriate to assume that
under all circumstances all of the various methods should
provide directly congruent results. There are several reasons
for this but two key issues are: (i) some of the methods are
inherently much more sensitive than others, thus, less
sensitive methods would obviously fail to verify relatively
small changes that can be detected by more sensitive methods,
and (ii) while some of the methods query the very same
parameter of lipid metabolism, this is not the case for all of
the methods. For example, the total amount of fat in two
mutants may be precisely the same but distributed very
differently among tissues or subcellular compartments. Such a
difference would obviously only emerge if the methods
employed preserve tissue and organellar integrity.
Below, we will first briefly describe the various methods
that have been employed to examine lipid metabolism in
C. elegans and then provide our perspective on their
weaknesses and strengths, which we have summarized in
Table 1. A technical description of each of the methods can be
found in reference (Barros et al., 2012). We wish to point out
that several investigators in the field may disagree with our
views on this topic.

Fixation and whole mount staining of C. elegans using
alcoholic solutions of Sudan Black B was the first employed

content. While in principle fixed staining should work as well
in C. elegans as in mammalian tissue culture cells or tissue
sections, the whole mount nature of the methodology imposes
some complications. Because of their thick, cross-linked,

Vital dye methods
One of the great advantages of C. elegans is that it is possible
to visualize fat depots in the transparent bodies of live
animals. Feeding worms their E. coli diet mixed with various
vital dyes, such as Nile Red, or BODIPY-labeled fatty acids
(BODIPY-FA), leads to accumulation of these fluorescent
dyes in various subcellular compartments, some of which are
lipid droplets while others are lysosome related organelles
(Mullaney et al., 2010; O’Rourke et al., 2009; Schroeder
et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010a). An advantage of vital dye
labeling over fixed staining is the minimal sample prepar-
ation required, the lower variability between samples, large
dynamic range and minimally invasive imaging. These
features enable quantitative, robust, high-throughput deter-
minations to be performed that are maximally compatible
with forward genetic strategies.
Nile Red is a dye that exhibits a strong dipole moment in
its excited state whose energy level is very sensitive to the
polarity of its surrounding solvent matrix. Solvent matrices of
increasing polarity lead to increasingly red-shifted emission
spectra and a weakening of the quantum yield of fluorescence,
with Nile Red being virtually non-fluorescent when dissolved
in a polar, protic solvent such as water (Greenspan & Fowler,
1985). This enables high-contrast imaging in living systems
where lipids are present, because in a lipid matrix the dye is
strongly fluorescent. However, the effects of lipid polarity are
still observed in the emission spectra of the dye. For example,
Nile Red produces a 560–580 nm peak emission when in
environments dominated by TAGs or very low-density
lipoproteins. A red shifted 620–640 nm peak emission is
produced by Nile Red when in environments enriched in

Caenorhabditis elegans cultured on low concentrations of
Nile Red exhibit preferential staining of intestinal granules,
those with BODIPY-FA exhibit intestinal staining but also
that of hypodermal depots (Figure 1A and B). When using
these low concentrations of Nile Red, the labeled intestinal
structures are not lipid droplets but acidic organelles known
as gut granules. These granules are distinct from lysosomes
since they lack key molecular markers of true lysosomes
(O’Rourke et al., 2009). The red-shifted 620–640 nm emis-
sion peak for Nile Red stained gut granules (Yen et al., 2010;
Figure 1B) is consistent with the staining of a depot rich in
polar lipids (e.g. mono- or di-glycerides, phospholipids, free
fatty acids) and distinct from other intestinal depots that are
observed by fixed staining methods (Brooks et al., 2009).
However, by simply elevating the concentration of Nile Red
to the low lM range during vital labeling, as it is employed in
vital staining of mammalian cells (Greenspan et al., 1985),
and in the fixed staining in C. elegans (Brooks et al., 2009),
intestinal, hypodermal and gonad lipid depots that exhibit
a peak fluorescence emission intensity of 570–580 nm
Figure 1(C and D) (Mullaney et al., 2010) are illuminated.
This is consistent with the emission intensity of Nile Red
dissolved in a strongly hydrophobic medium consisting of
triglycerides or cholesterol esters (Figure 1C and D). It is
unclear why low concentrations of Nile Red selectively label
gut granules. We speculate that the partition of low concen-
trations of Nile Red to gut granules may reflect normal
transitions of lipids among different cell biological compart-
ments rather than intrinsic differences in the physical
chemical properties of various lipid containing depots.
Indeed, in peroxisome-deficient mutants, low concentrations
of Nile Red label structures only accessible to higher (lM)
concentrations of this dye (Zhang et al., 2010a). Similarly,
when BODIPY is employed as a vital dye in C. elegans it
initially partitions to lipid droplets (e.g. upon 20 minutes of
exposure) but then accumulates in gut granules during
prolonged (18 h) exposures (Klapper et al., 2011).
Nile Red staining of gut granules has been interpreted
to suggest that this vital dye is irrelevant for analysis of
C. elegans lipid metabolism. Nevertheless, differences in gut
granule Nile Red staining have led to identification of
numerous evolutionarily conserved fat regulatory genes and
small molecules that affect fat metabolism when queried
through a variety of independent methodologies (Chen et al.,
2009; Cohen et al., 2009; Lemieux et al., 2011; Mullaney
et al., 2010; Pathare et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2008;
Van Gilst et al., 2005b). Some investigators have interpreted
this as pure coincidence. However, we think that there is an
intimate but poorly understood relationship between the gut
granules and various other lipid containing depots of
C. elegans. One possibility is that gut granules are involved
in degradative processes. This possibility is suggested by the
observations that enzymes that degrade lipids or cleave lipids
from various backbones localize to Nile Red staining gut
granules. For example, the phospholipase IPLA-2 localizes to
these granules during fasting and inactivation of this gene
leads to increased Nile Red staining (Huang et al., 2014).
Similarly, the activity of several acid lipases that affect overall
lipid metabolic processes likely localize to Nile Red staining
granules (Lapierre et al., 2011; O’Rourke & Ruvkun, 2013;
Wang et al., 2008).
Biochemical methods
Any type of dye binding assay is, at best, an indirect,
correlative measurement of the lipids it is attempting to
measure. Most major classes of lipids in C. elegans can be
measured directly via extraction and analytical chemistry
techniques such as thin layer chromatography (TLC) or gas
chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) of methanol
saponified lipid extracts (Srinivasan et al., 2008; Watts and
Browse, 2006). While TLC is limited to detecting changes in
abundance among major classes of lipids (e.g. triglycerides,
monoacyl glycerides, free fatty acids, etc.), GC/MS enables
quantification of individual fatty acid species.

A limitation of these extraction-based measurements is that
they are intrinsically whole organism, and population-based
measurements. This makes them relatively more variable and
less sensitive compared to vital dye and label free methods
(below). One factor contributing to the relative variability of
the population and extraction-based methods is that one
cannot guarantee that precisely the same number of animals is
present in each population and that the extractions are done
with precisely the same efficiency. Therefore, measurements
of extracted triglycerides must be normalized to some other
parameter, generally to either protein or phospholipids. Based
on our experience, a significant source of variation comes
from differential extractions of proteins or phospholipids.
Another factor is that the biochemical methods are essentially
multistep metabolomic measurements over variations with an
associated biological and technical variation, which necessi-
tates multiple determinations of
independent biological
samples for accurate measurement (Noack & Wiechert,
2014). In even the strongest mutations that change triglyceride
content in C. elegans for instance, that associated with a
hypomorphic mutation in the insulin receptor-like molecule
encoded by daf-2, a 2-3-fold change is typically observed.
Many more genes are likely to have physiologically conse-
quential effects that provoke a less dynamic change in
triglycerides which require 43 independent experiments to
yield statistically meaningful data. When using biochemical
methods another key consideration, which we will discuss
in more depth in the next section, is that lipids exist in
multiple forms, e.g. lipid droplets, yolk, and in multiple tissues,
e.g. intestine, germline, hypodermis. The mechanisms that
allocate lipids to different tissues or subcellular locations have
a large degree of physiological relevance with consequences
that impact human disease. These processes are largely
obscured in biochemical measures of whole organism lipid
extracts.
However, despite these limitations, the biochemical meth-
ods can provide certain unique insights. The ability to identify
specific lipid species of varying chain lengths and saturation
can be exploited to pinpoint roles of specific metabolic
enzymes, for example those of fatty acid desaturases or

Label free methods
An exciting development over the past several years has been
the application of Raman-based vibrational microscopy
techniques to the analysis of C. elegans fat (Folick et al.,
2011).
Vibrational
imaging
is
typically
employed
on
C. elegans via two distinct techniques termed Coherent
Anti-Raman Stokes (CARS) imaging and Stimulated Raman
Scattering (SRS) microscopy (Hellerer et al., 2007; Le et al.,
2010; Wang et al., 2011). Both techniques are compatible
with live, anesthetized C. elegans samples and work by
excitation of particular Raman vibrational frequencies of
endogenous biomolecules although they depend on distinct
optical configurations and measure different features of the
Raman emission. For a more in-depth review of these
techniques please see a recent review (Min et al., 2011). To
image
lipid
depots,
the
C-H
stretching
frequency
of
2845 cm1 is typically excited. While C-H bonds are not
unique to lipids in a biological system, they are at their
highest concentration in lipid rich cell biological depots such
as lipid droplets. This differential in C-H concentration
provides the contrast for this label free imaging technique.
Because
the
underlying
process
relies
on
two-photon
mixing, both techniques have excellent resolution and optical
sectioning capability. While CARS microscopy is an older
technique having been employed by multiple labs for the
imaging of C. elegans fat, the SRS measurements offer some
advantages over CARS albeit with the cost and technical
difficulties associated with a more complicated optical setup.
In particular, raw CARS images have an associated non-
resonant background, which must be subtracted to identify the
resonant features that are of interest. This non-resonant
background is absent from the SRS signal making raw SRS
images quite clear (Wang et al., 2011). CARS signals are
non-linearly related to the underlying signal generating
substance while, the SRS signal exhibits linear dependence
on underlying resonant bonds. These factors simplify the
extraction of quantitative features from SRS images over
CARS (Wang et al., 2011). A methodology based on
two-photon
microscopy
and
3rd

and SRS-based methods that can be performed with more
widely available equipment to the research community
(Tserevelakis et al., 2014)

methods is to utilize Raman-active labels as molecular probes
for specific structures within C. elegans (Fu et al., 2014). The
carbon-deuterium (C-D) stretching frequency occurs at a
relatively transparent part of the Raman spectrum in bio-

from
intrinsic
biological
species.
Worms
labeled
with

probes into their lipid deposits (Fu et al., 2014), opening up
the possibility of studying sub-cellular and inter-tissue lipid
dynamics which will be of great value to the field. The chief
limitations of the technique appear to be its sensitivity,
requiring C-D concentrations on the order of 100 lM for
detection (Fu et al., 2014).
Unresolved issues in interpretation of C. elegans
fat measurements
Several unresolved issues are pervasive in the C. elegans fat
literature and shade interpretations of some of the existing
data. These issues are interrelated and revolve around the fact
that C. elegans lipid depots exist in different compartments in
several different tissues.
Equating the intestine, the main fat depot of
C. elegans, to adipocytes, the main fat depot
of mammals
Given that the C. elegans intestine is rather large, researchers,
including us, who rely on visualization of fat depots in intact
animals through vital or fixed stains or those that rely on label
free methods have mostly focused on fat content of intestinal
cells. The intestine is the site of dietary lipid uptake as well as
its packaging for transport to other tissues. Most notably, the
intestine is the site of production of yolk, a lipoprotein particle
that is used for transferring nutrients from the hermaphrodite
to its developing embryos (Kimble & Sharrock, 1983).
Additional lipoprotein complexes also likely exist in this
organelle for transport of lipids to other tissues such as the
hypodermis. Based on these functions, the C. elegans intestine
may share more in common with the mammalian intestine and
liver than with adipocytes. We speculate that the hypodermal
skin-cells of C. elegans may function as the site of long-term
fat storage. Based on CARS microscopy it was estimated that
the hypodermal deposits account for 10–40% of the lipid
signals in the organism (Hellerer et al., 2007).
Treating various neutral lipid depots of the worm
intestine as equivalent and hence a readout of fat
storage of the worm
A related consideration is that the different fat depots of the
intestine may have drastically different functions from one
another. Electron microscopy images of the C. elegans
intestine reveal several classes of electron translucent droplets
with varying degrees of electron-dense material in their
interior (Figure 2A), also see (Zhang et al., 2010b). One
possibility is that these structures correspond to different
stages of yolk formation. Immuno-gold labeling of yolk in the
C. elegans intestine seems to mark similar partially electron
translucent structures (Paupard et al., 2001). Moreover, lipid

molecular markers that can definitively identify all yolk
particles. For example, dual fluorescence/CARS imaging of
transgenic C. elegans expressing translational fusions of the
yolk protein VIT2:GFP has revealed that that VIT-2 particles
and CARS positive structures in C. elegans intestines are
largely distinct (Yi et al., 2014). However, this does not rule
out a model where many of the CARS positive structures are
maturing yolk particles with sub-threshold detectable level of
VIT-2:GFP, particularly since VIT-2 is only one of a series of
vitellogenin-like proteins that are used during the process of
yolk formation. Even though vitellogenins are accepted
molecular markers of yolk, a global proteomic study of
C. elegans lipid droplets indicated that vitellogenins were the
most abundant proteins in the purified lipid droplets (Zhang
et al., 2012). In short, while a significant fraction, if not
most, of the lipid deposits in the intestine may be yolk, which
has a drastically different function than stored fats, most of
the studies of C. elegans fat content have not attempted to
account for this.
Contribution of the germ-line to extractable lipids
Another related issue that is particularly relevant to the
interpretation of biochemical extractions of triglycerides is
that the germline contains a significant amount of lipids that
are deposited in it through intestine-derived yolk (Grant &
Hirsh, 1999; Hall et al., 1999; Sharrock et al., 1990). During
larval development, in addition to the growth of the soma, the
organogenesis of the gonad and subsequent reproductive
period as an adult should be expected to be major destinations
for lipid flux in C. elegans. Indeed, during peak reproduction
in C. elegans the gonad is capable of producing a number of
progeny per day equivalent to the body mass of the parent
(Byerly et al., 1976). Importantly, these embryos are con-
tained and developing within the body of hermaphrodites and
thus contribute to total amount of extracted lipids. As the
somatic tissue of origin of all of the neutral lipids of the
developing progeny is the intestine, the vast majority of lipids
extracted from hermaphrodites is likely to be those of
intestinal yolk or lipid deposited in embryos as opposed to
lipid storage that can be used for somatic tissue needs of
C. elegans.
This situation is further complicated in animals with
defects in fecundity. Consider the cases of germ-line deficient
glp-1 mutants or insulin signaling deficient daf-2 animals,
both of which have dramatically elevated lipid levels in
their intestinal cells (O’Rourke et al., 2009). The excess fat of
glp-1 mutants has been generally interpreted as an increase in
fat storage of the animals, a situation that is difficult to
reconcile with the noted increases in lipase and autophagic
activities of these mutants (Lapierre et al., 2011; Wang
et al., 2008). However, it is possible that the excess fat
extracted from of these animals reflects a continued produc-
tion of yolk, perhaps at the expense of storage depots. Unlike
wild type animals, the absence of a germline as a destination
for yolk would result in intestinal accumulation of yolk,
which cannot easily be distinguished from intestinal lipid
depots.

Unresolved issues and key considerations
All of these observations point to an important question: do
most of extractable triglycerides from C. elegans truly
represent stores of energy to be used for somatic energetic
demands during periods of nutrient deprivation or do they
represent anabolic components intended for progeny produc-
tion or tissue maintenance? One might argue that even if the
latter is true during periods of nutrient deprivation they could
still be used as stores of metabolic fuel. There is however no
evidence for this. C. elegans is a species whose evolutionary
survival is driven by r-type reproductive strategy (Riddle
et al., 1997). Once the animals are past the dauer diapause
their metabolic output may be dominated by the production of
progeny at the expense of the soma. Indeed, even starved
animals continue to produce viable progeny albeit at a
dramatically reduced rate (Seidel & Kimble, 2011) which
indicates that the anabolic component of triglyceride metab-
olism persists even during periods of starvation. These
observations do not imply that fat storage in C. elegans is
only geared to progeny production. However, we neither know
which fat stores nor the proportion of fat in the organism that
is in transit versus being stored, as static images obtained by a
variety of methods lack that important data. Future experi-
ments using technology potentially capable of imaging the
dynamics of fat stores in different tissues and subcellular
depots (Fu et al., 2014) should help resolve some of these
questions.
In spite of the observed intra- and inter-cellular complex-
ities in C. elegans lipid handling, a large number of
investigators continue to treat fat content in C. elegans as if
it is a homogeneous entity. Indeed, the term ‘‘fat mass’’ has
been used to describe the total extractable triglycerides from
whole animals. This reduces all of the intracellular and
intercellular complexity of lipid handling, utilization and
storage into a single value: up, down or unchanged. Treating
the fat content of C. elegans as a homogeneous depot
obfuscates the diverse physiological origins of various
fat depots. In this context, concepts from mammalian fat
biology are instructive. Fat mass in mammals is generally
determined by measuring adipose fat content, which is
indeed the principle depository of mammalian triglycerides,
rather than homogenizing all of the mammalian tissues
together
in
service
of
triglyceride
measurements.
By
analogy,
the
current
conceptualization
of
fat
mass
of
C. elegans may be more akin to determining triglycerides
extracted from a whole mouse bearing two thirds of its
overall body mass in the liver and germline! Much of the
organism’s metabolic flux in this mythical mouse model of
C. elegans would be derived from liver-directed anabolic
support of reproduction rather than maintenance of energy
homeostasis of the soma. Moreover, in mammals, it is
readily appreciated that obesity is associated with increased
levels of plasma lipoproteins or fatty liver. Yet, it is also
readily appreciated that there may be elevated levels of
plasma lipoproteins or fatty liver in the absence of obesity.
Similarly, under conditions of food deprivation it is readily
accepted that mammalian adipocytes may be losing stored
triglyceride while fat content of mammalian liver may go up
as this tissue is a central transit hub for lipid transport
(Lin et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 2010).
In short, we believe that recognizing the diversity of lipid
handling subcellular compartments, whether they be lipid
droplets, yolk, or lysosome related organelles, as well as the
likelihood that triglyceride pools in different tissues may have
different functions, can only enrich the field by allowing for
investigation of how each of these lipid compartments relate
to one another and the dynamic regulation of lipid homeo-
stasis across tissues. Thus, each of the different methods for
querying lipid biology in C. elegans should be recognized as
suited for different purposes and should not be expected to
produce identical results under all conditions.
Summary
Common molecular mechanisms have been found to shape
development in organisms with dramatically different mor-
phological features. In a similar manner, the recognition that
fat regulation is a physiological process suggests its mech-
anisms must have deep evolutionary roots. As in any other
organism, C. elegans must coordinate its metabolic, physio-
logical, and behavioral responses based on changing nutri-
tional supplies and energetic demands for various cellular and
organism’s functions. Over a decade ago, perusing the
sequenced genome of C. elegans already indicated that
many of the known mammalian fat and feeding pathways have
molecular counterparts in this organism. The past decade has
seen functional verification of this notion, but more import-
antly, has provided the time whereby experimental advantage
of C. elegans can be leveraged to search for previously
uncharacterized fat regulatory pathway that are then be shown
to retain analogous functions in mammals. It is our opinion
that analyses of C. elegans fat would benefit from the
recognition that in this organism, as in mammals, there is a
diversity of lipid rich compartments and tissues that likely
have dramatically different functions. Ultimately, disentan-
gling the various strands of this complexity is critical to
understanding organism’s fat homeostasis, its relationship to
mechanisms of aging as well as various other biological
processes that are intertwined with metabolism.
